title: Three Plays Left
passages:
The Marrow groaned in her lines, hull kissing the Kettle's concrete flank with every swell. Storm bell hammered from the arcology's crown — three strikes, pause, three strikes — and the channel current ran thick with debris: broken pallets, a shipping container's corner, the bloated white of something that had once been a dog. Tide marks on the gate's steel ribs showed maybe forty minutes before the lock teeth engaged and the Stair drowned for the season.

Wren sat in the cabin's aft corner, slate cradled in both hands. Salt crust feathered its edges. The recorder's housing had flooded at forty-two meters, pressure forcing brine through every seal, and the works whined when she tilted it — a sound like a dying insect. Salas sat opposite, berth book open on his knees, pen frozen mid-stroke. He hadn't spoken since they'd surfaced. Fourteen months in an air pocket had hollowed him to a thing that breathed and watched and waited.

"Three plays," Wren said, not looking up. "Maybe two if the salt's eaten the second head. After that it's brick." She thumbed the contact clean on her sleeve, pressed the actuator. "Everyone who needs to hear this, get in here."

Dey appeared in the companionway first, scrubber harness dangling from one hand, the other braced against the frame. His chest rattled — wet, deep, the sound of lungs that had traded their last clean air for a boy named Teo. Nia slipped in behind him, Teo tucked against her hip, the boy's fingers knotted in her shirt. Bayo leaned in the hatch, bandaged hands tucked into his armpits, calling the surge timing to Sol up on deck. Sol came last, rain-slick oilskin dripping on the deck plates, eyes moving from Wren to Salas to the slate and back.

"Play it," Sol said.

The speaker crackled. Static swallowed the cabin, thick and wet. The crew leaned in.
